title: Socratic Self-Questioning
subtitle: You hold beliefs about your market, your customers, and your business that you have never
useWhen: seriously tested. These beliefs shape your decisions without you realising it. Some of them are correct. Some are expensive assumptions masquerading as facts.
howToUse: Socratic questioning named after Socrates' method of rigorous intellectual inquiry through probing questions is a structured technique for examining beliefs, uncovering assumptions, and testing the logic of conclusions. Applied as a self-examination tool, it becomes one of the most powerful mental models a founder can use: before committing to a strategic direction, a major hire, or a significant investment, you ask a series of questions designed to expose what you actually believe and why. AI makes this practice available on demand a rigorous thinking partner that will push back without ego.
steps: Use Socratic questioning on your most confident beliefs, not your uncertainties. Confidence is where blind spots hide.
Ask AI to steelman the opposite position before you commit to your view.
Write your reasoning before the session, vague beliefs survive questioning; explicit ones do not.

Run this exercise before any major strategic decision, not after it. Challenge your own thinking before it becomes your strategy AI won't push back without ego" is the pitch, but it can just as easily mirror your confidence back to you unless you explicitly ask it to argue the other side.
origin: Socratic method — ancient Greek philosophy — applied to business strategic thinking
promptBody:
Act as a Socratic questioner. Your role is to rigorously examine my thinking through
probing questions — not to agree or validate. Push back on weak logic.
Belief or decision to examine:
[STATE THE BELIEF, PLAN, OR DECISION YOU WANT TO TEST]
Apply the six categories of Socratic questions:
CLARIFICATION  :  What exactly do I mean by this? Can I give a concrete example?
ASSUMPTIONS    :  What am I taking for granted here? What would have to be true  
                                   for this to hold?
EVIDENCE            :  What is my evidence for this belief? How strong is it — anecdote  
                                   or data?
PERSPECTIVE     :  How would a sceptic view this? What is the strongest opposing  
                                  argument?
IMPLICATIONS   :  If this is true, what else must be true? What are the consequences 
                                  if I am wrong?
QUESTIONING THE QUESTION: Is this the right question? What is the deeper question
underneath it?
End with: the one assumption I should validate before committing to this belief.

proTip:
The most important Socratic question is "What would have to be true for me to be
wrong?" This forces you to define the falsifiability of your belief - the conditions under
which you would update your view. A belief that cannot be proven wrong isn't a belief, it's
a story you've decided not to test.
